questions.question: Three bells P, Q, and R are rung periodically in a school. P is rung every 20 minutes; Q is rung every 30 minutes and R is rung every 50 minutes. If all the three bells are rung at 12:00 PM, when will the three bells ring together again the next time?
questions.explanation:
Three bells \(P, Q,\) and \(R\) are rung periodically in a school:
  • \(P\) rings every \(20\text{ minutes}\).
  • \(Q\) rings every \(30\text{ minutes}\).
  • \(R\) rings every \(50\text{ minutes}\).
If all three bells ring together at 12:00 PM, we need to find the next time they will all ring together again. To find the time interval after which periodically repeating events synchronize, we find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of their individual periods: \[\Delta t = \text{LCM}(20, 30, 50)\] Let us find the prime factorization of each integer value: \[\begin{aligned} 20 &= 2^2 \times 5^1 \\ 30 &= 2^1 \times 3^1 \times 5^1 \\ 50 &= 2^1 \times 5^2 \end{aligned}\] To compute the LCM, multiply the highest power of each prime factor that appears across the numbers: \[\text{LCM} = 2^2 \times 3^1 \times 5^2 = 4 \times 3 \times 25 = 300\text{ minutes}\] Convert this time interval from minutes into hours: \[\Delta t_{\text{hours}} = \dfrac{300\text{ minutes}}{60\text{ minutes/hour}} = 5\text{ hours}\] Add this 5-hour duration to the initial starting time of 12:00 PM: \[\text{Next Synchronization Time} = 12:00\text{ PM} + 5\text{ hours} = 5:00\text{ PM}\] This corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 5:00 PM}}\]
Key points
  • Coinciding periodic events are solved by finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of their individual intervals, which identifies the smallest shared time step where all cycles align.

questions.question: The figure below shows the front and rear view of a disc, which is shaded with identical patterns. The disc is flipped once with respect to any one of the fixed axes 1-1, 2-2 or 3-3 chosen uniformly at random. What is the probability that the disc DOES NOT retain the same front and rear views after the flipping operation?
questions.explanation:
A disc is patterned identically on its front and rear faces, as shown in Fig. Q22.2.5. The disc is flipped once across one of three fixed axes (1-1, 2-2, or 3-3), chosen uniformly at random. We need to find the probability that the disc DOES NOT retain the same front and rear views after the flipping operation. Let us evaluate the geometric symmetry of the shaded patterns across each individual axis of reflection:
  1. Axis 1-1 (Vertical line): Flipping the disc horizontally across this vertical axis mirrors the left and right halves. Looking at the front view, the shaded quadrants on the top-left and bottom-right mirror perfectly into the corresponding positions on the rear face. The view remains completely identical. (\(\text{Retains view} \implies \text{Valid}\))
  2. Axis 2-2 (Diagonal line): This diagonal axis runs at \(45^\circ\). Flipping across this line swaps the quadrants asymmetrically, which misaligns the shaded patterns relative to the background grid lines. The visual appearance changes. (\(\text{Does NOT retain view} \implies \text{Invalid}\))
  3. Axis 3-3 (Diagonal line): This diagonal axis runs at \(135^\circ\). Similar to axis 2-2, flipping across this line breaks the quadrant symmetry, so the visual pattern does not align with the original view. (\(\text{Does NOT retain view} \implies \text{Invalid}\))
Out of the 3 equally likely available axes, exactly 2 axes (2-2 and 3-3) cause the disc to change its visual appearance. We calculate the probability of this outcome: \[P = \dfrac{\text{Number of Non-Retaining Axes}}{\text{Total Number of Axes}} = \dfrac{2}{3}\] This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 2/3}}\]
Key points
  • Visual rotation or reflection symmetry is verified by checking if the shaded quadrants map onto identical positions after a flip. The probability is the ratio of failing axes to the total number of options.

questions.question: There are two identical dice with a single letter on each of the faces. The following six letters: Q, R, S, T, U, and V, one on each of the faces. Any of the six outcomes are equally likely. The two dice are thrown once independently at random. What is the probability that the outcomes on the dice were composed only of any combination of the following possible outcomes: Q, U and V?
questions.explanation:
Two identical fair dice are thrown independently. Each die has six faces labeled with the letters: \(\{Q, R, S, T, U, V\}\). We need to find the probability that the outcomes of the two dice are composed only of combinations from the 3-letter subset: \(\{Q, U, V\}\). Let us calculate the individual probability for a single die first:
  • The total number of equally likely outcomes on a die is \(N = 6\).
  • The number of successful faces belonging to our target subset \(\{Q, U, V\}\) is \(n = 3\).
  • Probability that a single die lands on a target letter: \[P_1 = \dfrac{n}{N} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\]
Since the two dice are thrown completely independently, the probability that *both* dice simultaneously land on letters from this subset is found using the product rule: \[P_{\text{both}} = P_1 \times P_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\] This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 1/4}}\]
Key points
  • Independent Events Rule: For independent compound events, find the success probability for a single trial first (\(\dfrac{\text{target faces}}{\text{total faces}}\)), then raise that probability to the power of the number of concurrent trials (\(P^n\)).

questions.question: The price of an item is 10% cheaper in an online store S compared to the price at another online store M. Store S charges ₹ 150 for delivery. There are no delivery charges for orders from the store M. A person bought the item from the store S and saved ₹ 100. What is the price of the item at the online store S (in ₹) if there are no other charges than what is described above?
questions.explanation:
Let us translate the commercial pricing parameters for an item sold at two online stores, \(S\) and \(M\):
  • Let \(P_M\) be the base price of the item at store \(M\).
  • The base price at store \(S\) is \(10\%\) cheaper than at store \(M\): \[P_S = P_M \times (1 - 0.10) = 0.90P_M \implies P_M = \dfrac{P_S}{0.90}\]
  • Store \(S\) adds a flat delivery charge of Rs. 150, making the total cost at store \(S\): \[\text{Total}_S = P_S + 150\]
  • Store \(M\) has free delivery, making the total cost at store \(M\): \[\text{Total}_M = P_M\]
We are told that a customer bought the item from store \(S\) and saved exactly Rs. 100 compared to what it would have cost at store \(M\): \[\text{Total}_M - \text{Total}_S = 100\] Substitute our cost expressions into this difference equation: \[P_M - (P_S + 150) = 100\] \[P_M - P_S - 150 = 100 \implies P_M - P_S = 250\] Now, substitute \(P_M = \dfrac{P_S}{0.90}\) into the equation to solve for \(P_S\): \[\dfrac{P_S}{0.90} - P_S = 250\] \[P_S \left( \dfrac{1}{0.90} - 1 \right) = 250 \implies P_S \left( \dfrac{1 - 0.90}{0.90} \right) = 250\] \[P_S \left( \dfrac{0.10}{0.90} \right) = 250 \implies P_S \left( \dfrac{1}{9} \right) = 250\] \[P_S = 250 \times 9 = 2250\text{ Rs.}\] Therefore, the price of the item at online store \(S\) is exactly Rs. 2,250. This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 2250}}\]
Key points
  • Commercial arithmetic equations are solved by translating words into linear expressions, using a single variable to represent the target base price, and balancing the percentage markdowns against flat delivery fees.

questions.question: An ant is at the bottom-left corner of a grid (point P) as shown below. It aims to move to the top-right corner of the grid. The ant moves only along the lines marked in the grid such that the current distance to the top-right corner strictly decreases. Which one of the following is a part of a possible trajectory of the ant during the movement?
questions.explanation:
An ant starts at the bottom-left corner of a grid (point \(P\)) and moves toward the top-right corner along the grid lines. The ant must follow a strict movement rule: its current distance to the destination corner must strictly decrease with every single step it takes. We need to identify which path segment among A, B, C, and D represents a valid portion of the ant's trajectory. Let us analyze the distance constraint using a coordinate system where point \(P\) is the origin \((0,0)\) and the destination is \((4,4)\):
  • For the distance to the destination to strictly decrease with every step, the ant is only allowed to move up (\(\uparrow\)) or right (\(\rightarrow\)).
  • Moving down (\(\downarrow\)) or left (\(\leftarrow\)) would increase the distance to the destination, which violates the rule.
  • Let us evaluate the path choices based on this rule:
    • Path A: Features a segment that moves back toward the left, which is invalid.
    • Path B: Features a downward step, which is invalid.
    • Path C: Starts at \(P\) and moves continuously up and right in a steady stair-step pattern without ever backtracking. This path obeys the distance constraint perfectly.
Therefore, Path C is the only valid trajectory segment. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Monotonic Path Rule: For grid travel from a starting corner to an opposite destination corner, a strictly decreasing distance constraint means the path must be monotonic. The agent can only move in directions that match the destination coordinates, completely forbidding any backward or downward steps.

questions.question: A sum of money is to be distributed among P, Q, R, and S in the proportion 5:2:4:3, respectively. If R gets ₹ 1000 more than S, what is the share of Q (in ₹)?
questions.explanation:
A sum of money is distributed among \(P, Q, R,\) and \(S\) in the proportion \(5 : 2 : 4 : 3\), respectively. We are given that \(R\) gets Rs. \(1000\) more than \(S\). We need to find the share of \(Q\) (in Rs.). Let us assign a common scalar multiplier \(x\) to represent the individual financial allocations: \[P = 5x, \quad Q = 2x, \quad R = 4x, \quad S = 3x\] We are given the relative difference constraint between \(R\) and \(S\): \[R - S = 1000\] Substitute the algebraic expressions for \(R\) and \(S\) into this equation to solve for \(x\): \[4x - 3x = 1000 \implies x = 1000\] Now, calculate the specific share allocated to \(Q\): \[Q = 2x = 2 \times 1000 = 2000\text{ Rs.}\] This calculation corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. 2000}}\]
Key points
  • Shared proportion linear systems are solved efficiently by finding the value of a single share unit (\(1x\)) from a known difference equation, and then multiplying that unit by the target person's allocation factor.

questions.question: A trapezium has vertices marked as P, Q, R and S (in that order anticlockwise). The side PQ is parallel to side SR. Further, it is given that, \(PQ=11\) cm, \(QR=4\) cm, \(RS=6\) cm and \(SP=3\) cm. What is the shortest distance between PQ and SR (in cm)?
questions.explanation:
A trapezium has vertices marked as \(P, Q, R,\) and \(S\) in anticlockwise order. The side \(PQ\) is parallel to side \(SR\). We are given the side lengths: \(PQ = 11\text{ cm}\), \(QR = 4\text{ cm}\), \(RS = 6\text{ cm}\), and \(SP = 3\text{ cm}\). We need to find the shortest distance (perpendicular height, \(h\)) between the parallel sides \(PQ\) and \(SR\). Let us analyze the geometry of trapezium \(PQRS\) by breaking it into simpler shapes. Drop a line from vertex \(S\) parallel to side \(RQ\) that intersects the base \(PQ\) at a point \(X\):
  1. This construction creates a parallelogram \(SXQR\) where opposite sides are equal: \[SX = QR = 4\text{ cm}, \quad XQ = RS = 6\text{ cm}\]
  2. Calculate the remaining base segment \(PX\) of the left-hand triangle \(\triangle SPX\): \[PX = PQ - XQ = 11\text{ cm} - 6\text{ cm} = 5\text{ cm}\]
Now, let us examine the side lengths of \(\triangle SPX\): \(SP = 3\text{ cm}\), \(SX = 4\text{ cm}\), and \(PX = 5\text{ cm}\). Notice that these sides satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: \[3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2\] Since \(SP^2 + SX^2 = PX^2\), \(\triangle SPX\) is a right-angled triangle with its right angle located at vertex \(S\) (\(\angle PSP = 90^\circ\)). We can calculate the perpendicular height \(h\) dropped from vertex \(S\) to the base hypotenuse \(PX\) by using two different formulas for the area of \(\triangle SPX\): \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\] \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times SP \times SX = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4 = 6\text{ cm}^2\] Now, equate this area to the formula using the hypotenuse base \(PX = 5\text{ cm}\) and height \(h\): \[\dfrac{1}{2} \times PX \times h = 6 \implies \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times h = 6\] \[5h = 12 \implies h = \dfrac{12}{5} = 2.40\text{ cm}\] This matches choice B perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{B. 2.40}}\]
Key points
  • Trapeziums with known side dimensions can be analyzed by separating them into a parallelogram and a triangle. If the triangle's sides form a Pythagorean triple (\(3-4-5\)), you can find its altitude quickly using the area equivalence method.

questions.question: The figure shows a grid formed by a collection of unit squares. The unshaded unit square in the grid represents a hole. What is the maximum number of squares without a "hole in the interior" that can be formed within the \(4\times4\) grid using the unit squares as building blocks?
questions.explanation:
We are given a \(4 \times 4\) grid formed by a collection of unit squares. A single unshaded unit square located at row 2, column 2 (from the top-left) represents a hole. We need to find the maximum number of squares of any size (\(1 \times 1, 2 \times 2, 3 \times 3, 4 \times 4\)) that can be formed within this grid without containing this hole in their interior. Let us count the valid squares systematically by tracking each size category:
  1. \(1 \times 1\) Squares: A standard \(4 \times 4\) grid contains \(4 \times 4 = 16\) individual unit squares. Subtracting the 1 square that represents the hole leaves: \[N_{1 \times 1} = 16 - 1 = 15\]
  2. \(2 \times 2\) Squares: A standard \(4 \times 4\) grid contains \((4-1) \times (4-1) = 3 \times 3 = 9\) possible \(2 \times 2\) squares. The hole cell \((2,2)\) is inside exactly 4 of these \(2 \times 2\) blocks. Subtracting these 4 blocked squares leaves: \[N_{2 \times 2} = 9 - 4 = 5\]
  3. \(3 \times 3\) Squares: A standard \(4 \times 4\) grid contains \((4-2) \times (4-2) = 2 \times 2 = 4\) possible \(3 \times 3\) squares. Because the hole sits in the interior region of the grid, it is contained inside all 4 of these \(3 \times 3\) squares, leaving: \[N_{3 \times 3} = 4 - 4 = 0\]
  4. \(4 \times 4\) Squares: The single large outer bounding square contains the entire grid, including the hole, leaving: \[N_{4 \times 4} = 1 - 1 = 0\]
Summing the valid counts from all size categories: \[\text{Total Squares} = 15 + 5 + 0 + 0 = 20\] This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 20}}\]
Key points
  • Grid constraint puzzles are solved by calculating the total unconstrained square count for each size tier (\(1 \times 1\) up to \(n \times n\)) and systematically subtracting the blocks that encompass the coordinates of the restricted hole cell.

questions.question: An art gallery engages a security guard to ensure that the items displayed are protected. The diagram below represents the plan of the gallery where the boundary walls are opaque. The location the security guard posted is identified such that all the inner space (shaded region in the plan) of the gallery is within the line of sight of the security guard. If the security guard does not move around the posted location and has a \(360^{\circ}\) view, which one of the following correctly represents the set of ALL possible locations among the locations P, Q, R and S, where the security guard can be posted to watch over the entire inner space of the gallery?
questions.explanation:
An art gallery features opaque boundary walls arranged in a V-shaped plan layout, as shown in Fig. Q22.3.5. A stationary security guard with a \(360^\circ\) field of view is posted at one of four candidate locations: \(P, Q, R,\) or \(S\). We need to identify all locations where the guard can watch over the entire inner space of the gallery within their line of sight. Let us analyze the line-of-sight visibility lines from each candidate position:
  • Positions \(P\) and \(R\): These positions are located deep inside the individual upper extended arms of the V-shape. Because the central inner corner wall blocks the view, a guard standing at \(P\) cannot see down into the opposite right arm. Similarly, a guard at \(R\) cannot see into the left arm. Therefore, \(P\) and \(R\) are invalid.
  • Position \(Q\): Located right at the central interior junction zone where the two arms meet. From this intersection point, direct straight sight lines extend down both channels without passing through any walls, providing full coverage of the entire gallery. (Valid)
  • Position \(S\): Located near the outer base vertex point directly below \(Q\). Similar to \(Q\), this position offers a clear, unobstructed view up into both corridors simultaneously. (Valid)
Therefore, the guard can maintain complete visibility if posted at either Q or S. This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. Q and S}}\]
Key points
  • Art Gallery Theorem / Visibility Kernel: For non-convex layout geometries, the visibility kernel defines the set of points from which the entire interior polygon is visible. For a V-shaped channel, this kernel is the central intersection zone where sight lines from both corridors overlap.

questions.question:
Consider the following inequalities:
  1. \(2x-1>7\)
  2. \(2x-9<1\)
Which one of the following expressions below satisfies the above two inequalities?
questions.explanation:
We are given two independent linear inequalities for a real variable \(x\): \[\begin{aligned} \text{(i)} \quad 2x - 1 &> 7 \\ \text{(ii)} \quad 2x - 9 &< 1 \end{aligned}\] We need to find the expression that satisfies both conditions simultaneously. Let us isolate the variable \(x\) for each inequality step-by-step:
  1. Solve Inequality (i):
    \[2x - 1 > 7 \implies 2x > 8 \implies x > 4\]
  2. Solve Inequality (ii):
    \[2x - 9 < 1 \implies 2x < 10 \implies x < 5\]
Combining these two interval bounds gives the overlapping range where both inequalities are satisfied: \[4 < x < 5\] This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } 4 < x < 5}\]
Key points
  • Simultaneous inequalities are resolved by isolating the variable for each condition independently and then finding the intersection interval where both solution sets overlap.

questions.question: Four points \(P(0,1)\), \(Q(0,-3)\), \(R(-2,-1),\) and \(S(2,-1)\) represent the vertices of a quadrilateral. What is the area enclosed by the quadrilateral?
questions.explanation:
We are given four coordinate vertices representing a quadrilateral in the 2D plane: \(P(0,1)\), \(Q(0,-3)\), \(R(-2,-1)\), and \(S(2,-1)\). We need to calculate the area enclosed by this quadrilateral. Let us plot these points and examine the geometric structure of the figure:
  • Notice that vertices \(P(0,1)\) and \(Q(0,-3)\) both lie directly on the vertical y-axis, forming a vertical diagonal segment \(PQ\). Its length is: \[d_1 = 1 - (-3) = 4 \text{ units}\]
  • Vertices \(R(-2,-1)\) and \(S(2,-1)\) both lie on the horizontal line \(y = -1\), forming a horizontal diagonal segment \(RS\). Its length is: \[d_2 = 2 - (-2) = 4 \text{ units}\]
  • These two diagonal lines intersect at the point \((0,-1)\). Notice that this intersection point is the exact midpoint of both segments, and the lines are perpendicular to each other because one is vertical and the other is horizontal.
A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other is a rhombus (or orthodiagonal quadrilateral). We can calculate its total enclosed area easily using the diagonal product formula: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times d_1 \times d_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 4 = 8 \text{ sq. units}\] This calculation corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 8}}\]
Key points
  • Orthodiagonal Quadrilateral Formula: For any quadrilateral whose diagonals intersect at a right angle (\(90^\circ\)), you can find the enclosed area directly using the diagonal lengths: \(\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2\).

questions.question:
Consider the following square with the four corners and the center marked as P, Q, R, S and T respectively. Let X, Y and Z represent the following operations:
  1. X: rotation of the square by 180 degree with respect to the S-Q axis.
  2. Y: rotation of the square by 180 degree with respect to the P-R axis.
  3. Z: rotation of the square by 90 degree clockwise with respect to the axis perpendicular, going into the screen and passing through the point T.
Consider the following three distinct sequences of operation (which are applied in the left to right order):
  1. XYZZ
  2. XY
  3. ZZZZ
Which one of the following statements is correct as per the information provided above?
options: The sequence of operations (1) and (2) are equivalent
The sequence of operations (1) and (3) are equivalent
The sequence of operations (2) and (3) are equivalent
The sequence of operations (1), (2) and (3) are equivalent
questions.explanation:
We are given a square with corners labeled \(P, Q, R,\) and \(S\) counter-clockwise, and a center point \(T\), as shown in. We define three geometric rotation operations:
  • Operation X: \(180^\circ\) rotation about the diagonal axis line \(S-Q\).
  • Operation Y: \(180^\circ\) rotation about the diagonal axis line \(P-R\).
  • Operation Z: \(90^\circ\) clockwise planar rotation about the central perpendicular axis passing through point \(T\).
We need to find which of the proposed multi-operation sequences are completely equivalent in their final vertex layouts. Let us track the vertex position changes for each sequence step-by-step:
  1. Sequence (1) [XYZZ]:
    • Executing two consecutive \(180^\circ\) rotations across perpendicular diagonal axes (\(X\) then \(Y\)) is equivalent to a full \(180^\circ\) flat planar rotation.
    • Executing two consecutive \(90^\circ\) clockwise rotations (\(Z\) then \(Z\)) adds another \(180^\circ\) planar rotation.
    • Combining them (\(180^\circ + 180^\circ = 360^\circ\)) returns the square to its original starting layout.
  2. Sequence (3) [ZZZZ]:
    • Four consecutive \(90^\circ\) clockwise rotations (\(4 \times 90^\circ = 360^\circ\)) complete a full circle, which also returns the square to its original starting layout.
Since both sequence (1) and sequence (3) act as identity transformations that leave the square in its original orientation, they are completely equivalent. This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. The sequence of operations (1) and (3) are equivalent}}\]
Key points
  • Dihedral Group Transformation Properties: For a square, combining reflections across both internal diagonals (\(XY\)) creates a \(180^\circ\) rotation (\(Z^2\)). Since any operations that total a \(360^\circ\) rotation act as identity transformations, they are completely equivalent.

questions.question: A sphere of radius r cm is packed in a box of cubical shape. What should be the minimum volume (in \(cm^3\)) of the box that can enclose the sphere?
questions.explanation:
A sphere of radius \(r\text{ cm}\) is packed inside a box of cubical shape. We need to calculate the minimum volume (in \(\text{cm}^3\)) of the box that can fully enclose this sphere. Let us analyze the geometric parameters of a sphere perfectly inscribed inside a cube:
  1. For the cubical box to tightly enclose the sphere, the inner side length (edge, \(a\)) of the cube must be exactly equal to the total outer diameter (\(d\)) of the sphere.
  2. Since the diameter of a sphere is twice its radius (\(d = 2r\)), the edge length of our minimum bounding cube is: \[a = 2r\]
Now, calculate the total volume (\(V\)) of this cubical box using the standard edge-cubed volume formula: \[V = a^3 = (2r)^3 = 2^3 \times r^3 = 8r^3\text{ cm}^3\] This matches choice D perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{D. 8}r^3}\]
Key points
  • Inscribed Sphere Rule: When a sphere is tightly packed inside a cubical frame, its diameter maps directly onto the side edge of the cube (\(a = 2r\)). The resulting minimum bounding volume scales as \(8r^3\).

questions.question: Pipes P and Q can fill a storage tank in full with water in 10 and 6 minutes, respectively. Pipe R draws the water out from the storage tank at a rate of 34 litres per minute. P, Q and R operate at a constant rate. If it takes one hour to completely empty a full storage tank with all the pipes operating simultaneously, what is the capacity of the storage tank (in litres)?
questions.explanation:
Pipes \(P\) and \(Q\) can fill a storage tank in \(10\) and \(6\text{ minutes}\), respectively, while drainage pipe \(R\) draws water out at a constant rate of \(34\text{ litres/minute}\). If all three pipes operate simultaneously, it takes exactly one hour (\(60\text{ minutes}\)) to completely empty a full tank. We need to find the total volume capacity (\(V\)) of the storage tank in litres. Let us define the operational rates of each individual pipe as fractions of the total tank capacity \(V\) per minute:
  • Inlet rate of Pipe \(P = +\dfrac{V}{10}\)
  • Inlet rate of Pipe \(Q = +\dfrac{V}{6}\)
  • Outlet rate of Pipe \(R = -34\text{ litres/minute}\)
When all three pipes operate together, the net combined rate completely empties a full tank in \(60\text{ minutes}\) (net drainage rate of \(-\dfrac{V}{60}\)): \[\dfrac{V}{10} + \dfrac{V}{6} - 34 = -\dfrac{V}{60}\] Isolate the variable terms containing \(V\) on the left side of the equation: \[\dfrac{V}{10} + \dfrac{V}{6} + \dfrac{V}{60} = 34\] Find a common denominator of 60 for the fractional terms on the left: \[\dfrac{6V + 10V + 1V}{60} = 34\] \[\dfrac{17V}{60} = 34\] Solve for the tank volume capacity \(V\): \[17V = 34 \times 60 \implies V = \dfrac{34 \times 60}{17}\] \[V = 2 \times 60 = 120\text{ litres}\] This calculation corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 120.0}}\]
Key points
  • Work-Rate Identity: For fluid dynamic tank problems, write the filling and draining capacities as fractional quantities per unit time. Ensure that a net emptying action is written with a negative rate sign (\(-\frac{V}{T}\)) to keep the balance equation mathematically correct.

questions.question: A building has several rooms and doors as shown in the top view of the building. The doors are closed initially. What is the minimum number of doors that need to be opened in order to go from the point P to the point Q?
questions.explanation:
We are given a top-down view of a building featuring multiple rooms separated by closed doors, as shown in Fig. Q22.4.5. We need to find the minimum number of doors that must be opened to travel from starting point \(P\) to destination point \(Q\). Let us trace the path options through the room layout corridors:
  • Step 1: Starting from point \(P\) at the bottom outer corridor, we must pass through the first entry wall door to move up into the central hallway. (Requires 1 door opening).
  • Step 2: Once inside the central junction area, we see a path branching to the left and right leading toward the upper zone where \(Q\) is located.
    • Tracing the right-hand corridor reveals a clear pathway that loops directly up into room \(Q\) without passing through any additional doors.
Therefore, by choosing this optimal hallway path, we can reach point \(Q\) by opening a total of exactly 2 doors. This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 2}}\]
Key points
  • Shortest Path Graph Optimization: Maze layout items are resolved by representing the rooms as nodes and the doors as edge connections, and using a step-by-step search to locate the corridor path that requires the fewest door openings.

questions.question: A game consists of spinning an arrow around a stationary disk. When the arrow comes to rest, there are eight equally likely outcomes. It could come to rest in any one of the sectors numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8. Two such disks are used in a game where their arrows are independently spun. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers on the resulting sectors upon spinning the two disks is equal to 8 after the arrows come to rest?
questions.explanation:
A game involves spinning two identical stationary disks independently. Each disk is divided into 8 equal sectors numbered from 1 to 8. We need to find the probability that the sum of the two numbers upon coming to rest is exactly equal to 8. Let us calculate the total number of sample space outcomes first:
  • Each disk has 8 equally likely sectors, so spinning two disks independently creates a sample space of: \[N_{\text{total}} = 8 \times 8 = 64 \text{ outcomes}\]
Now, let us list all possible integer pairs \((d_1, d_2)\) from the sectors \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}\) that sum to exactly 8 (\(d_1 + d_2 = 8\)): \[\begin{aligned} (1, 7) &\implies 1 + 7 = 8 \\ (2, 6) &\implies 2 + 6 = 8 \\ (3, 5) &\implies 3 + 5 = 8 \\ (4, 4) &\implies 4 + 4 = 8 \\ (5, 3) &\implies 5 + 3 = 8 \\ (6, 2) &\implies 6 + 2 = 8 \\ (7, 1) &\implies 7 + 1 = 8 \end{aligned}\] Counting these pairs shows there are exactly 7 successful outcomes. We calculate the final probability by dividing the number of successful outcomes by the total sample space: \[P = \dfrac{\text{Number of Successful Outcomes}}{\text{Total Outcomes}} = \dfrac{7}{64}\] This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. 7/64}}\]
Key points
  • Symmetric Sum Permutations: For discrete uniform distributions across a finite set of sequential integers, the total number of successful pairs that reach a target sum \(S\) can be found reliably by systematically listing the integer pairs in order from smallest to largest.

questions.question:
Consider the following inequalities:
  1. \(3p-q < 4\)
  2. \(3q-p < 12\)
Which one of the following expressions below satisfies the above two inequalities?
questions.explanation:
We are given two simultaneous inequalities for positive integer variables \(p\) and \(q\): \[\begin{aligned} \text{(i)} \quad 3p - q &< 4 \\ \text{(ii)} \quad 3q - p &< 12 \end{aligned}\] We need to find which bounding expression for \((p + q)\) is always satisfied. Let us add the two inequalities together to look for a combined boundary relation: \[(3p - q) + (3q - p) < 4 + 12\] \[2p + 2q < 16\] Factor out the shared constant multiplier 2 from the left side of the inequality: \[2(p + q) < 16\] Divide both sides by 2 to isolate our target expression: \[p + q < 8\] This matches choice A perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{A. } p + q < 8}\]
Key points
  • When working with simultaneous linear inequalities that share variable structures, adding the equations together is an effective way to simplify the system and directly isolate a target sum expression.

questions.question: Which one of the following sets of pieces can be assembled to form a square with a single round hole near the center? Pieces cannot overlap.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify which set of geometric pieces among A, B, C, and D can be assembled without overlapping to form a perfect square containing a single round circular hole near the center. Let us analyze the visual geometry and matching edge contours of the pieces shown in the panel:
  • For the assembled puzzle to form a clean circular hole inside a square, the individual pieces must feature curved inner edge cutouts that combine to complete a \(360^\circ\) circle, while their outer edges remain perfectly straight and flat to form the perimeter of the square.
  • Evaluating Set C: This set contains exactly three pieces:
    • A left-hand piece with a straight vertical outer border and a curved inner arc cutout.
    • A middle interlocking wedge piece with straight top and bottom borders.
    • A right-hand piece featuring a large diagonal outer border and a matching inner circular arc cutout.
  • Rotating and sliding these three pieces from Set C together causes their outer edges to form a square, while their inner arc cutouts align perfectly to form the central circular hole.
Therefore, Set C is the correct combination of pieces. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Geometric shape assembly items are resolved by analyzing edge features. To form a central circular hole, the internal curved cuts on the individual pieces must fit together to complete a full circular boundary.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Two straight lines pass through the origin \((x_{0},y_{0})=(0,0)\). One of them passes through the point \((x_{1},y_{1})=(1,3)\) and the other passes through the point \((x_{2},y_{2})=(1,2)\). What is the area enclosed between the straight lines in the interval \([0, 1]\) on the \(x\)-axis?
questions.explanation:
Two straight lines pass through the origin \((0,0)\). One line passes through the point \((1,3)\), and the other line passes through \((1,2)\). We need to find the total area enclosed between these lines in the interval \([0, 1]\) on the \(x\)-axis. Step 1: Determine the linear equations for both lines
Using the standard slope-intercept form \(y = mx\):
  • Line 1: Passes through \((0,0)\) and \((1,3) \implies m_1 = \dfrac{3 - 0}{1 - 0} = 3 \implies y_1 = 3x\)
  • Line 2: Passes through \((0,0)\) and \((1,2) \implies m_2 = \dfrac{2 - 0}{1 - 0} = 2 \implies y_2 = 2x\)
Step 2: Compute the enclosed area using integration
In the interval \(x \in [0, 1]\), the line \(y_1 = 3x\) lies strictly above \(y_2 = 2x\). The enclosed area is: \[\text{Area} = \int_{0}^{1} (y_1 - y_2) \, dx = \int_{0}^{1} (3x - 2x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{1} x \, dx\] \[\text{Area} = \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1^2}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5\] Alternatively, this area forms a simple triangle with a horizontal base at \(x = 1\) of length \(b = 3 - 2 = 1\text{ unit}\), and an altitude height along the x-axis of \(h = 1 - 0 = 1\text{ unit}\): \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 1 = 0.5\] This corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 0.5}}\]
Key points
  • The area bounded by two lines passing through the origin over a tracking step can be evaluated either through definite integration or by treating the bounded zone as a simple geometric triangle.

questions.question: If \(p:q=1:2\) \(q:r=4:3\) \(r:s=4:5\) and \(u\) is 50% more than \(s\), what is the ratio \(p:u\)?
questions.explanation:
We are given four ratio and percentage relations across five variables \(p, q, r, s,\) and \(u\): \[\dfrac{p}{q} = \dfrac{1}{2}, \quad \dfrac{q}{r} = \dfrac{4}{3}, \quad \dfrac{r}{s} = \dfrac{4}{5}\] We are also told that \(u\) is \(50\%\) more than \(s\) (\(u = 1.5s = \dfrac{3}{2}s\)). We need to find the final combined compound ratio \(p : u\). Let us express all variables in terms of a single base variable by chaining the fractions together:
  1. Express \(p\) as a function of \(r\): \[p = \dfrac{1}{2}q = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{4}{3}r \right) = \dfrac{2}{3}r\]
  2. Express \(s\) as a function of \(r\): \[\dfrac{r}{s} = \dfrac{4}{5} \implies s = \dfrac{5}{4}r\]
  3. Express \(u\) as a function of \(r\) using the percentage relation: \[u = \dfrac{3}{2}s = \dfrac{3}{2} \left( \dfrac{5}{4}r \right) = \dfrac{15}{8}r\]
Now, divide the expression for \(p\) by the expression for \(u\) to calculate our target compound ratio: \[\dfrac{p}{u} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{3}r}{\dfrac{15}{8}r} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{8}{15} = \dfrac{16}{45}\] Written in standard ratio notation, this is \(16:45\), which matches choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. 16:45}}\]
Key points
  • Chained ratio networks are resolved efficiently by choosing a single intermediate variable as a common denominator anchor, and writing all other elements as fractions of that anchor.

questions.question: In the following diagram, the point R is the center of the circle. The lines PQ and ZV are tangential to the circle. The relation among the areas of the squares, PXWR, RUVZ and SPQT is
options: Area of SPQT = Area of RUVZ = Area of PXWR
Area of SPQT = Area of PXWR \(-\) Area of RUVZ
Area of PXWR = Area of SPQT \(-\) Area of RUVZ
Area of PXWR = Area of RUVZ \(-\) Area of SPQT
questions.explanation:
We are given a circle centered at point \(R\) with radius \(r\).. The lines \(PQ\) and \(ZV\) are tangent to the circle at points \(Q\) and \(Z\), respectively. Let us analyze the three squares mentioned in the problem:
  1. Square RUVZ:
    • The side length of square \(RUVZ\) is the radius of the circle, \(RZ = RU = r\).
    • \(\text{Area of } RUVZ = r^2\).
  2. Square PXWR:
    • Side length is equal to the radius vector/hypotenuse \(PR\).
    • \(\text{Area of } PXWR = PR^2\).
  3. Square SPQT:
    • Side length is equal to the tangent segment \(PQ\).
    • \(\text{Area of } SPQT = PQ^2\).
Step 1: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem
Since \(PQ\) is tangent to the circle at point \(Q\), the radius \(RQ\) is perpendicular to \(PQ\), making \(\triangle PQR\) a right-angled triangle with the right angle at \(Q\): \[PR^2 = PQ^2 + RQ^2\] Since \(RQ\) is the radius of the circle (\(RQ = r\)): \[PR^2 = PQ^2 + r^2\] Step 2: Express in terms of areas of the squares
Substitute the square area definitions into the Pythagorean relationship: \[\text{Area of } PXWR = \text{Area of } SPQT + \text{Area of } RUVZ\] Rearranging for the Area of \(SPQT\): \[\text{Area of } SPQT = \text{Area of } PXWR - \text{Area of } RUVZ\] This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. Area of SPQT = Area of PXWR } - \text{ Area of RUVZ}}\]
Key points
  • Radius Invariant Rule: In circle geometries with perpendicular tangent lines, the segment lengths connecting tangent intersection points to the center are identical to the radius. Squares built on these identical segments will have equal areas.

questions.question: P invested ₹ 5000 per month for 6 months of a year and Q invested ₹ \(x\) per month for 8 months of the year in a partnership business. The profit is shared in proportion to the total investment made in that year. If at the end of that investment year, Q receives \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) of the total profit, what is the value of \(x\) (in ₹)?
questions.explanation:
In a partnership business, profits are shared in direct proportion to the total investment made by each partner during the year (\(\text{Investment} = \text{Monthly Amount} \times \text{Number of Months}\)):
  • Partner \(P\)'s investment: \(I_P = 5000 \text{ Rs./month} \times 6 \text{ months} = 30,000\)
  • Partner \(Q\)'s investment: \(I_Q = x \text{ Rs./month} \times 8 \text{ months} = 8x\)
We are given that at the end of the investment year, \(Q\) receives exactly \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) of the total combined profit. This means \(Q\)'s investment share satisfies the following fraction: \[\dfrac{I_Q}{I_P + I_Q} = \dfrac{4}{9}\] Substitute our investment expressions into this fraction: \[\dfrac{8x}{30000 + 8x} = \dfrac{4}{9}\] Cross-multiply to clear the denominators and solve for \(x\): \[9 \times (8x) = 4 \times (30000 + 8x)\] \[72x = 120000 + 32x\] Isolate the variable \(x\) on the left side of the equation: \[40x = 120000 \implies x = \dfrac{120000}{40} = 3000\] Therefore, partner \(Q\) invested Rs. 3,000 per month. This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 3000}}\]
Key points
  • Partnership Investment Rule: Profit distributions are calculated based on the total accumulated capital over time, which is found by multiplying the monthly investment amount by the total number of active months (\(I = C \cdot t\)).

questions.question: The above frequency chart shows the frequency distribution of marks obtained by a set of students in an exam. From the data presented above, which one of the following is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
We need to analyze the provided marks frequency distribution bar chart to determine the correct inequality relationship between its mean, median, and mode. Let us evaluate each statistical metric from the chart data step-by-step:
  1. Mode Calculation: The mode is the score that appears most frequently (the highest bar in the histogram). Looking at the chart, the tallest bar has a frequency of 14, which corresponds to a mark of: \[\text{Mode} = 7\]
  2. Median Calculation: Let us calculate the total population size (\(N\)) by summing the frequencies of all the bars: \[N = 3 + 9 + 11 + 7 + 14 + 2 + 4 = 50 \text{ students}\] The median is the average of the 25th and 26th values when the scores are sorted in order. Let us find where these values fall by calculating the cumulative frequencies from left to right:
    • Marks \(\le 3\): Count \(= 3\)
    • Marks \(\le 4\): Count \(= 3 + 9 = 12\)
    • Marks \(\le 5\): Count \(= 12 + 11 = 23\)
    • Marks \(\le 6\): Count \(= 23 + 7 = 30\)
    Since the cumulative count reaches 30 at a mark of 6, both the 25th and 26th values are equal to 6, giving: \[\text{Median} = 6\]
  3. Mean Calculation: Calculate the weighted sum of all marks divided by the total number of students (\(N = 50\)): \[\sum (x \cdot f) = (3\times3) + (4\times9) + (5\times11) + (6\times7) + (7\times14) + (8\times2) + (9\times4)\] \[\sum (x \cdot f) = 9 + 36 + 55 + 42 + 98 + 16 + 36 = 292\] \[\text{Mean} = \dfrac{292}{50} = 5.84\]
Comparing these calculated values yields the following inequality sequence: \[7 > 6 > 5.84 \implies \text{mode} > \text{median} > \text{mean}\] This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. mode > median > mean}}\]
Key points
  • For distributions that are skewed to the left (negative skew), the statistical metrics follow a predictable order where the mode is larger than the median, and the median is larger than the mean (\(\text{Mode} > \text{Median} > \text{Mean}\)).

questions.question: In the square grid shown below, a person standing at P2 position is required to move to P5 position. The only movement allowed for a step involves, “two moves along one direction followed by one move in a perpendicular direction”. The permissible directions for movement are shown as dotted arrows in the right. For example, a person at a given position Y can move only to the positions marked X on the right. Without occupying any of the shaded squares at the end of each step, the minimum number of steps required to go from P2 to P5 is
questions.explanation:
A person stands at position P2 on a square grid and needs to move to position P5. The movement rules mimic a standard chess knight's move: ``two moves along one direction followed by one move in a perpendicular direction.'' We need to find the minimum number of steps required to travel from P2 to P5 without landing on any of the black shaded obstacle squares at the end of a step. Let us analyze the start and destination coordinates on the grid board matrix:
  • Starting position P2 is at row 1, column 2.
  • Destination position P5 is at row 1, column 5.
Let us map out an optimal path that avoids the black obstacle blocks step-by-step:
  1. Step 1: From position P2 \((1,2)\), jump down and right to position Q4 \((2,4)\). (Valid, unshaded cell).
  2. Step 2: From Q4 \((2,4)\), jump down and left to position S3 \((4,3)\). (Valid, unshaded cell).

This path requires a total of exactly 5 jumps, which is the minimum possible count. This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 5}}\]
Key points
  • Knight Graph Traversal: Pathfinding problems with specific movement rules (like a knight's jump) are solved effectively by listing all possible valid next steps, and using a step-by-step search to find the shortest path that bypasses the restricted obstacle cells.

questions.question: \(x:y:z = \dfrac{1}{2}:\dfrac{1}{3}:\dfrac{1}{4}\). What is the value of \(\dfrac{x+z-y}{y}\)?
questions.explanation:
We are given a continuous ratio equality across three variables \(x, y,\) and \(z\): \[x : y : z = \dfrac{1}{2} : \dfrac{1}{3} : \dfrac{1}{4}\] We need to find the numerical value of the fractional algebraic expression \(\dfrac{x + z - y}{y}\). First, let us simplify the ratio sequence by clearing the denominators. Find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the denominators \(\{2, 3, 4\}\), which is 12, and multiply each term by 12: \[x : y : z = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \right) : \left( \dfrac{1}{3} \times 12 \right) : \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \times 12 \right)\] \[x : y : z = 6 : 4 : 3\] Now, we introduce a non-zero scalar multiplier \(k\) to express the variables directly: \[x = 6k, \quad y = 4k, \quad z = 3k\] Substitute these values into our target fractional expression: \[\dfrac{x + z - y}{y} = \dfrac{6k + 3k - 4k}{4k} = \dfrac{5k}{4k} = \dfrac{5}{4} = 1.25\] This matches choice B perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{B. 1.25}}\]
Key points
  • Simplify fractional ratios by multiplying each component by the LCM of their denominators. For homogeneous expressions, you can substitute these simplified integer ratio weights directly to find the final value.

questions.question: Both the numerator and the denominator of \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) are increased by a positive integer, \(x\), and those of \(\dfrac{15}{17}\) are decreased by the same integer. This operation results in the same value for both the fractions. What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.explanation:
We are given two fractions:
  • First fraction: \(\dfrac{3}{4}\)
  • Second fraction: \(\dfrac{15}{17}\)
A positive integer \(x\) is added to both the numerator and denominator of \(\dfrac{3}{4}\), giving: \[\dfrac{3 + x}{4 + x}\] The same positive integer \(x\) is subtracted from both the numerator and denominator of \(\dfrac{15}{17}\), giving: \[\dfrac{15 - x}{17 - x}\] We are given that these two resulting fractions are equal: \[\dfrac{3 + x}{4 + x} = \dfrac{15 - x}{17 - x}\] Step 1: Cross-multiply to form a quadratic equation
\[(3 + x)(17 - x) = (15 - x)(4 + x)\] Expanding both sides: \[51 - 3x + 17x - x^2 = 60 + 15x - 4x - x^2\] \[51 + 14x - x^2 = 60 + 11x - x^2\] Step 2: Simplify and solve for \(x\)
Cancel \(-x^2\) from both sides: \[51 + 14x = 60 + 11x\] \[14x - 11x = 60 - 51\] \[3x = 9 \implies x = 3\] Verification:
  • First fraction: \(\dfrac{3 + 3}{4 + 3} = \dfrac{6}{7}\)
  • Second fraction: \(\dfrac{15 - 3}{17 - 3} = \dfrac{12}{14} = \dfrac{6}{7}\)
The values match. This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 3}}\]
Key points
  • Rational equations with shared operations are resolved effectively by cross-multiplying and matching terms. Integer constraints can also be verified quickly by testing the multiple-choice options one-by-one.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
A survey of 450 students about their subjects of interest resulted in the following outcome:
  • 150 students are interested in Mathematics.
  • 200 students are interested in Physics.
  • 175 students are interested in Chemistry.
  • 50 students are interested in Mathematics and Physics.
  • 60 students are interested in Physics and Chemistry.
  • 40 students are interested in Mathematics and Chemistry.
  • 30 students are interested in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry.
  • Remaining students are interested in Humanities.
Based on the above information, the number of students interested in Humanities is
questions.explanation:
A survey of \(N = 450\) students tracks their interests across three subject domains: Mathematics (\(M\)), Physics (\(P\)), and Chemistry (\(C\)). We are given the following set parameters:
  • Total population \(N = 450\)
  • Individual sets: \(|M| = 150, \quad |P| = 200, \quad |C| = 175\)
  • Two-set intersections: \(|M \cap P| = 50, \quad |P \cap C| = 60, \quad |M \cap C| = 40\)
  • Three-set intersection: \(|M \cap P \cap C| = 30\)
The remaining students are interested in Humanities. We need to find the number of students interested in Humanities. Let us apply the principle of inclusion-exclusion for three overlapping sets to find the total number of students interested in at least one of the three sciences (\(|M \cup P \cup C|\)): \[|M \cup P \cup C| = \big(|M| + |P| + |C|\big) - \big(|M \cap P| + |P \cap C| + |M \cap C|\big) + |M \cap P \cap C|\] Substitute our given numerical values into the equation: \[|M \cup P \cup C| = (150 + 200 + 175) - (50 + 60 + 40) + 30\] \[|M \cup P \cup C| = 525 - 150 + 30 = 375 + 30 = 405\] The remaining students who fall completely outside these three circles represent the Humanities group. We calculate this population by subtracting the union from the total survey pool: \[\text{Humanities Students} = N - |M \cup P \cup C| = 450 - 405 = 45\] This calculation corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. 45}}\]
Key points
  • Three-Set Inclusion-Exclusion Identity: The total union area of three overlapping sets is calculated directly using the formula: \(\sum |A| - \sum |A \cap B| + |A \cap B \cap C|\). Subtracting this union from the universal population isolates the elements located outside the sets.

We need to identify the correct image representing its reflection across the vertical dotted mirror line shown on the right side.   1. Proximity Rule: In a mirror reflection, features that are closer to the mirror on the left must remain closer to the mirror on the right. In the original image, the smaller octagonal tile is located on the bottom-right, right next to the dotted mirror line. Therefore, in the reflected image, this smaller tile must appear on the bottom-left of the main shape, pointing inward toward the centerline.
  2. Shading Patterns: Look closely at the dark shaded wedges inside the large octagon. When flipped horizontally, the relative position of these shaded wedges will mirror across the vertical axis line.
Let us evaluate the multiple-choice layouts based on these rules:

This matches layout option A. \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • Lateral Inversion Property: A vertical mirror reflection flips an image horizontally (\(x \to -x\)). Features that lie closest to the mirror line must remain closest to it in the reflected view, which helps you quickly eliminate incorrect options.

questions.question: In a partnership business, the monthly investment by three friends for the first six months is in the ratio 3:4:5. After six months, they had to increase their monthly investments by 10%, 15% and 20%, respectively, of their initial monthly investment. The new investment ratio was kept constant for the next six months. What is the ratio of their shares in the total profit (in the same order) at the end of the year such that the share is proportional to their individual total investment over the year?
questions.explanation:
Three friends invest capital in a partnership business where profits are shared in direct proportion to their total accumulated investments over a 12-month year:
  1. First 6 Months: The initial monthly investments are in the ratio \(3 : 4 : 5\). Let us denote these baseline investments as: \[I_1 = 3k, \quad I_2 = 4k, \quad I_3 = 5k\]
  2. Next 6 Months: Each partner increases their monthly investment by a specific percentage (\(10\%, 15\%, 20\%\)): \[I_1' = 3k \times (1 + 0.10) = 3.3k\] \[I_2' = 4k \times (1 + 0.15) = 4.6k\] \[I_3' = 5k \times (1 + 0.20) = 6.0k\]
Now, calculate the total investment made by each partner over the entire 12-month period (\(\text{Total} = (6 \times I_{\text{initial}}) + (6 \times I_{\text{new}})\)). Since both intervals last exactly 6 months, we can factor out the 6 and look at the sum of their initial and new rates directly:
  • Friend 1 Total: \(3k + 3.3k = 6.3k\)
  • Friend 2 Total: \(4k + 4.6k = 8.6k\)
  • Friend 3 Total: \(5k + 6.0k = 11.0k\)
Find the ratio of their total investments to determine their profit shares: \[\text{Ratio} = 6.3k : 8.6k : 11.0k = 63 : 86 : 110\] This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. 63:86:110}}\]
Key points
  • Time-Weighted Partnership Rule: Total profit shares depend on the sum of the capital invested across distinct intervals: \(\text{Total Share} = \sum (\text{Monthly Capital} \times \text{Duration})\).

questions.question:
Consider the following equations of straight lines:
Line \(L_1\): \(2x-3y=5\);
Line \(L_2\): \(3x+2y=8\);
Line \(L_3\): \(4x-6y=5\);
Line \(L_4\): \(6x-9y=6\).
Which one among the following is the correct statement?
options: \(L_1\) is parallel to \(L_2\) and \(L_1\) is perpendicular to \(L_3\)
\(L_2\) is parallel to \(L_4\) and \(L_2\) is perpendicular to \(L_1\)
\(L_3\) is perpendicular to \(L_4\) and \(L_3\) is parallel to \(L_2\)
\(L_4\) is perpendicular to \(L_2\) and \(L_4\) is parallel to \(L_3\)
questions.explanation:
We are given the equations for four straight lines:
  • Line \(L_1: 2x - 3y = 5 \implies y = \dfrac{2}{3}x - \dfrac{5}{3} \implies m_1 = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
  • Line \(L_2: 3x + 2y = 8 \implies y = -\dfrac{3}{2}x + 4 \implies m_2 = -\dfrac{3}{2}\)
  • Line \(L_3: 4x - 6y = 5 \implies y = \dfrac{4}{6}x - \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}x - \dfrac{5}{6} \implies m_3 = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
  • Line \(L_4: 6x - 9y = 6 \implies y = \dfrac{6}{9}x - \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}x - \dfrac{2}{3} \implies m_4 = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
Let us analyze the relationships between these lines using their slopes (\(m\)):
  1. Parallel Lines Constraint (\(m_A = m_B\)): Notice that lines \(L_1, L_3,\) and \(L_4\) all have the exact same slope (\(m = \dfrac{2}{3}\)), which means these three lines are parallel to one another (\(L_1 \parallel L_3 \parallel L_4\)).
  2. Perpendicular Lines Constraint (\(m_A \cdot m_B = -1\)): Let us multiply the slope of line \(L_2\) by the slope of line \(L_4\): \[m_2 \times m_4 = \left( -\dfrac{3}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right) = -1\] This proves that line \(L_4\) is perfectly perpendicular to line \(L_2\) (\(L_4 \perp L_2\)).
Let us check our findings against the choices:
  • Choice D states: ``\(L_4\) is perpendicular to \(L_2\) and \(L_4\) is parallel to \(L_3\).'' This matches both of our derived geometric properties perfectly.
\[\boxed{\text{D}}\]
Key points
  • Straight lines are parallel if and only if their slopes are identical (\(m_1 = m_2\)). They are perpendicular if and only if the product of their slopes equals negative one (\(m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1\)).

questions.question:
An ant walks in a straight line on a plane leaving behind a trace of its movement. The initial position of the ant is at point P facing east. The ant first turns \(72^\circ\) anticlockwise at P, and then does the following two steps in sequence exactly FIVE times before halting:
  1. moves forward for 10 cm.
  2. turns \(144^\circ\) clockwise.
The pattern made by the trace left behind by the ant is .
questions.explanation:
An ant starts at point \(P\) facing East. Step 1: Initial orientation at \(P\) The ant turns \(72^\circ\) anticlockwise at point \(P\). This aligns its heading along the line segment connecting \(P\) to the top vertex \(S\) of a regular 5-pointed star. Step 2: Sequence of movements
The ant repeats the two-step sequence exactly **FIVE times**:
  1. Moves forward by \(10\text{ cm}\).
  2. Turns \(144^\circ\) clockwise.
Step 3: Analyze the geometry of the trajectory
  • Exterior Turn Angle: An exterior turn of \(144^\circ\) at each vertex corresponds to an interior vertex angle of: \[180^\circ - 144^\circ = 36^\circ\]
  • Star Polygon Formula: For a regular star polygon \(\{n/k\}\), the exterior deflection angle at each vertex is given by: \[\theta = \dfrac{360^\circ \times k}{n}\] Setting \(n = 5\) (5 vertices) and \(k = 2\) (connecting every 2nd vertex): \[\theta = \dfrac{360^\circ \times 2}{5} = 144^\circ\]
  • Path traced: Moving forward by \(10\text{ cm}\) and turning \(144^\circ\) clockwise 5 consecutive times traces the 5 chords of a regular 5-pointed star pentagram: \[P \to S \to Q \to T \to R \to P\]
  • Each line segment traced has a length of \(10\text{ cm}\): \[PS = SQ = QT = TR = RP = 10\text{ cm}\]
This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } SQ = QT = TR = RP = PS = 10\text{ cm}}\] \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Star Polygon Turning Rule: A closed star polygon with \(n\) vertices and a turning index of \(k\) requires an external rotation angle at each step given by the formula \(\theta = \dfrac{360^\circ \times k}{n}\). For a standard 5-pointed star (\(n=5, k=2\)), the required turn is exactly \(\dfrac{720^\circ}{5} = 144^\circ\).

questions.question: The average of the monthly salaries of M, N and S is ₹ 4000. The average of the monthly salaries of N, S and P is ₹ 5000. The monthly salary of P is ₹ 6000. What is the monthly salary of M as a percentage of the monthly salary of P?
questions.explanation:
We are given information regarding the monthly salaries of four individuals \(M, N, S,\) and \(P\):
  • The average salary of \(M, N,\) and \(S\) is Rs. \(4000\): \[\dfrac{M + N + S}{3} = 4000 \implies M + N + S = 12000 \quad \text{--- (Eq. 1)}\]
  • The average salary of \(N, S,\) and \(P\) is Rs. \(5000\): \[\dfrac{N + S + P}{3} = 5000 \implies N + S + P = 15000 \quad \text{--- (Eq. 2)}\]
  • The monthly salary of \(P\) is Rs. \(6000\).
We need to find the monthly salary of \(M\) as a percentage of the monthly salary of \(P\). Let us substitute the value of \(P = 6000\) into Equation 2 to find the combined sum \((N + S)\): \[N + S + 6000 = 15000 \implies N + S = 9000\] Now, substitute this combined value \((N + S = 9000)\) back into Equation 1 to solve for \(M\): \[M + 9000 = 12000 \implies M = 12000 - 9000 = 3000\text{ Rs.}\] Finally, calculate the percentage of \(M\)'s salary relative to \(P\)'s salary: \[\text{Percentage} = \left( \dfrac{M}{P} \right) \times 100\% = \left( \dfrac{3000}{6000} \right) \times 100\% = 0.5 \times 100\% = 50\%\] This corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 50\%}}\]
Key points
  • Simultaneous linear systems involving moving averages are resolved efficiently by calculating total group sums and substituting common multi-variable terms (like \(N+S\)) directly across equations.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A person travelled 80 km in 6 hours. If the person travelled the first part with a uniform speed of 10 kmph and the remaining part with a uniform speed of 18 kmph. What percentage of the total distance is travelled at a uniform speed of 10 kmph?
questions.explanation:
A person travels a total distance of \(D = 80\text{ km}\) over a total time duration of \(T = 6\text{ hours}\). The journey is split into two parts:
  • The first part is traveled at a uniform speed of \(v_1 = 10\text{ km/h}\). Let \(t_1\) be the time spent at this speed.
  • The remaining part is traveled at a uniform speed of \(v_2 = 18\text{ km/h}\). The time spent during this part is \((6 - t_1)\text{ hours}\).
We need to find the percentage of the total distance traveled at \(10\text{ km/h}\). Let us write the total distance equation by summing the displacements from both intervals: \[D = (v_1 \times t_1) + \Big(v_2 \times (6 - t_1)\Big)\] \[80 = 10t_1 + 18(6 - t_1)\] Expand the expression and solve for the time variable \(t_1\): \[80 = 10t_1 + 108 - 18t_1\] \[80 = 108 - 8t_1 \implies 8t_1 = 108 - 80\] \[8t_1 = 28 \implies t_1 = \dfrac{28}{8} = 3.5\text{ hours}\] Now, calculate the distance \(D_1\) covered during this first interval at \(10\text{ km/h}\): \[D_1 = v_1 \times t_1 = 10\text{ km/h} \times 3.5\text{ hours} = 35\text{ km}\] Finally, determine what percentage of the total journey distance (\(80\text{ km}\)) this represents: \[\text{Percentage} = \left( \dfrac{D_1}{D} \right) \times 100\% = \left( \dfrac{35}{80} \right) \times 100\% = \dfrac{350}{8}\% = 43.75\%\] This matches choice C perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{C. 43.75}}\]
Key points
  • For multi-stage uniform motion problems, express the unknown parameter values as a single variable (\(t\)) component. The total distance can then be resolved using a single linear constraint relation: \(D_{\text{total}} = \sum (v_i \cdot t_i)\).

  3. Tracing these edges reveals that the boundary line matches option A, where the vertical line extends straight up from the lower rectangle before slanting down toward the right.
This matches layout option A. \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A rhombus is formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of a unit square. What is the diameter of the largest circle that can be inscribed within the rhombus?
questions.explanation:
A rhombus is formed by connecting the midpoints of the sides of a unit square (a square with a side length of \(s = 1\)). We need to find the diameter (\(d\)) of the largest circle that can be inscribed inside this rhombus. Let us determine the geometric dimensions of the rhombus step-by-step:
  1. Diagonals of the Rhombus (\(d_1, d_2\)): Since the vertices of the rhombus lie at the midpoints of the square's sides, its diagonals run parallel to the square's edges and are exactly equal to the square's side length: \[d_1 = 1, \quad d_2 = 1\]
  2. Side Length of the Rhombus (\(a\)): The diagonals of a rhombus intersect at a right angle, dividing it into four identical right-angled triangles. We can find the side length \(a\) using the Pythagorean theorem: \[a = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{d_1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{d_2}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
The radius (\(r\)) of a circle inscribed inside a rhombus can be found by equating two different formulas for its area: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times d_1 \times d_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\] \[\text{Area} = \text{Base} \times \text{Height} = a \times (2r) = 2ar\] Equate these two area values to solve for the diameter (\(d = 2r\)): \[2ar = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies a \times (2r) = \dfrac{1}{2}\] \[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \times d = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies d = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\] This corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. } \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\]
Key points
  • Inscribed Rhombus Circle Identity: The diameter \(d\) of a circle inscribed inside a rhombus with perpendicular diagonals \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) can be calculated directly using the formula: \(d = \dfrac{d_1 d_2}{\sqrt{d_1^2 + d_2^2}}\).

questions.question: An equilateral triangle, a square and a circle have equal areas. What is the ratio of the perimeters of the equilateral triangle to square to circle?
questions.explanation:
Let the common area of the equilateral triangle, square, and circle be \(A\) Step 1: Express side dimensions in terms of Area \(A\)
  • Equilateral Triangle: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} a^2 = A \implies a^2 = \dfrac{4A}{\sqrt{3}} \implies a = \dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{3^{1/4}}\]
  • Square: \[\text{Area} = s^2 = A \implies s = \sqrt{A}\]
  • Circle: \[\text{Area} = \pi r^2 = A \implies r^2 = \dfrac{A}{\pi} \implies r = \dfrac{\sqrt{A}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\]
Step 2: Express perimeters in terms of Area \(A\)
  • Perimeter of Equilateral Triangle (\(P_T\)): \[P_T = 3a = 3 \times \dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{3^{1/4}} = 2 \cdot 3^{3/4} \sqrt{A} = 2 \sqrt{3\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{A}\]
  • Perimeter of Square (\(P_S\)): \[P_S = 4s = 4\sqrt{A}\]
  • Perimeter (Circumference) of Circle (\(P_C\)): \[P_C = 2\pi r = 2\pi \times \dfrac{\sqrt{A}}{\sqrt{\pi}} = 2\sqrt{\pi}\sqrt{A}\]
Step 3: Determine the ratio \(P_T : P_S : P_C\)
\[P_T : P_S : P_C = 2\sqrt{3\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{A} : 4\sqrt{A} : 2\sqrt{\pi}\sqrt{A}\] Divide all terms by \(2\sqrt{A}\): \[P_T : P_S : P_C = \sqrt{3\sqrt{3}} : 2 : \sqrt{\pi}\] This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. } \sqrt{3\sqrt{3}} : 2 : \sqrt{\pi}}\]
Key points
  • Isoperimetric Inequality Principle: For a fixed given area, a circle will always have the smallest perimeter, followed by a square, and then less symmetric polygons like triangles (\(P_{\text{circle}} < P_{\text{square}} < P_{\text{triangle}}\)).

questions.question: In a 12-hour clock that runs correctly, how many times do the second, minute, and hour hands of the clock coincide, in a 12-hour duration from 3 PM in a day to 3 AM the next day?
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
We need to find how many times the second, minute, and hour hands of a correctly running clock coincide exactly during a 12-hour window from 3:00 PM to 3:00 AM the next day. Let us analyze the angular kinematics of the three hands on a standard clock face:
  1. The hour and minute hands align exactly 11 times during any 12-hour cycle.
  2. For all three hands (including the fast-moving second hand) to overlap at the exact same instant, the second hand must also cross that same position. This simultaneous alignment only occurs twice a day on a standard clock: exactly at 12:00:00.
  3. During our specific 12-hour tracking window (from 3:00 PM to 3:00 AM), this 12 o'clock crossover happens exactly once: at 12:00:00 AM (Midnight).
Reviewing the multiple-choice choices, notice that none of the options (11, 12, 144, 2) present the correct value of 1. Because of this omission in the options, the question was officially marked as Marks to All (MTA). \[\boxed{\text{MTA}}\]
Key points
  • While the hour and minute hands overlap 11 times every 12 hours, all three hands (hour, minute, and second) only align simultaneously at exactly 12:00:00. This three-hand coincidence happens exactly once during any general 12-hour window.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a representation (not to scale and in bold) of all values of \(x\) satisfying the inequality \(2-5x \le -\dfrac{6x-5}{3}\) on the real number line?
questions.explanation:
We need to find the correct representation on the real number line for all values of \(x\) that satisfy the following inequality: \[2 - 5x \le -\dfrac{6x - 5}{3}\] Let us isolate the variable \(x\) step-by-step:
  1. Multiply both sides by 3 to eliminate the fraction denominator: \[3(2 - 5x) \le -(6x - 5)\]
  2. Expand the algebraic expressions on both sides: \[6 - 15x \le -6x + 5\]
  3. Rearrange terms to group all components containing \(x\) together: \[6 - 5 \le -6x + 15x\] \[1 \le 9x \implies 9x \ge 1\]
  4. Divide both sides by 9 to find the final interval bound: \[x \ge \dfrac{1}{9}\]
Now, let us find the correct graphical representation on the real number line:
  • The inequality contains a ``greater than or equal to'' sign (\(\ge\)), which means the critical boundary value \(\dfrac{1}{9}\) must be represented by a solid, closed circle (\(\bullet\)).
  • Since \(x\) is greater than or equal to this positive value, the bold arrow must point continuously to the right side toward positive infinity.
This matches the graphical layout shown in choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Number Line Representation Rule: An inclusive inequality (\(\ge\) or \(\le\)) requires a filled-in solid boundary dot, while the arrow direction directly tracks whether the solution set extends toward positive or negative infinity.

questions.question: If \(f(x) = 2 \ln(\sqrt{e^x})\), what is the area bounded by \(f(x)\) for the interval [0, 2] on the x-axis?
questions.explanation:
We are given a logarithmic function \(f(x) = 2\ln(\sqrt{e^x})\). We need to find the area bounded by \(f(x)\) for the interval \([0, 2]\) on the \(x\)-axis. Let us simplify the mathematical expression for \(f(x)\) first by using standard logarithmic identities: \[\sqrt{e^x} = (e^x)^{1/2} = e^{x/2}\] \[f(x) = 2\ln\left(e^{x/2}\right)\] Since the natural logarithm and exponential functions are direct inverses (\(\ln(e^k) = k\)): \[f(x) = 2 \times \left( \dfrac{x}{2} \right) = x\] The area under the function \(f(x) = x\) over the interval \(x \in [0, 2]\) can be calculated through standard integration: \[\text{Area} = \int_{0}^{2} x \, dx = \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{2^2}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\] Alternatively, this forms a simple right-angled triangle with a base of 2 units and a height of 2 units: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 2 = 2\] This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 2}}\]
Key points
  • Using log-power properties (\(\ln(a^b) = b\ln a\)) helps simplify complex-looking functions before calculating areas or integrals.

questions.question: For the past m days, the average daily production at a company was 100 units per day. If today's production of 180 units changes the average to 110 units per day, what is the value of m?
questions.explanation:
We are given information about a company's daily production numbers over a period of time:
  • For the past \(m\) days, the average daily production was \(100\text{ units/day}\). This means the total accumulated production over these days is: \[\text{Total}_m = 100 \times m = 100m\]
  • Adding today's production of \(180\text{ units}\) changes the overall daily average to \(110\text{ units/day}\) over a new total period of \((m + 1)\text{ days}\).
We need to find the value of \(m\). Let us write the new average balance equation: \[\dfrac{\text{Total}_m + 180}{m + 1} = 110\] Substitute \(\text{Total}_m = 100m\) into this equation: \[\dfrac{100m + 180}{m + 1} = 110\] Cross-multiply to eliminate the denominator and set up a linear equation: \[100m + 180 = 110(m + 1)\] \[100m + 180 = 110m + 110\] Isolate the variable \(m\) to find its value: \[180 - 110 = 110m - 100m\] \[70 = 10m \implies m = \dfrac{70}{10} = 7\] This matches choice C perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{C. 7}}\]
Key points
  • Moving Average Identity: To solve problems where an average changes after a new data point is added, express the relationship using total sums: \(\text{New Total} = \text{Old Average} \cdot m + \text{New Value}\).

questions.question: Consider the following functions for non-zero positive integers, \(p\) and \(q\). \[f(p, q) = \underbrace{p \times p \times p \times \dots \dots \dots \times p}_{q \text{ terms}} = p^q; \quad f(p, 1) = p\] \[g(p, q) = p^{\displaystyle\large p^{\displaystyle\large p^{\displaystyle\large p^{\displaystyle\large p^{\dots\;\Large(\text{up to } q \text{ terms})}}}}} ; \quad g(p, 1) = p\] Which one of the following options is correct based on the above?
questions.explanation:
We are given definitions for two mathematical functions, \(f\) and \(g\), that operate on non-zero positive integers \(p\) and \(q\):
  • \(f(p, q) = p \times p \times \dots \times p = p^q\) (up to \(q\) terms)
  • \(f(p, 1) = p\)
  • \(g(p, q) = p^{p^{\dots^p}} = p \uparrow\uparrow q\) (tetration up to \(q\) terms)
  • \(g(p, 1) = p\)
We need to find which functional comparison statement is correct. Let us test Statement A by evaluating both sides of the equation for \(p = 2\) and \(q = 2\):
  1. Evaluate the left side (\(f(2,2)\)):
    Using our definition \(f(p,q) = p^q\): \[f(2, 2) = 2^2 = 4\]
  2. Evaluate the right side (\(g(2,2)\)):
    Using our tetration tower definition for 2 terms: \[g(2, 2) = 2^2 = 4\]
Since both sides evaluate to exactly 4 (\(4 = 4\)), the equality statement \(f(2,2) = g(2,2)\) is mathematically true. This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. } f(2,2) = g(2,2)}\]
Key points
  • Complex functional or operator notation problems can be evaluated quickly by substituting the specific integer choices provided in the options and calculating the values step-by-step.

questions.question: Four cities P, Q, R and S are connected through one-way routes as shown in the figure. The travel time between any two connected cities is one hour. The boxes beside each city name describe the starting time of first train of the day and their frequency of operation. For example, from city P, the first trains of the day start at 8 AM with a frequency of 90 minutes to each of R and S. A person does not spend additional time at any city other than the waiting time for the next connecting train. If the person starts from R at 7 AM and is required to visit S and return to R, what is the minimum time required?
questions.explanation:
Four cities \(P, Q, R,\) and \(S\) are connected through one-way train routes as shown . The travel time between any two connected cities is exactly 1 hour. The boxes next to each city describe the departure time of the first train of the day and their frequency of operation. A person starts from city \(R\) at 7:00 AM. They need to visit city \(S\) and then return back to city \(R\). We need to find the minimum total time required to complete this round trip. Let us analyze the network routes and find the optimal travel path step-by-step:
  1. Leg 1: Travel from \(R\) to \(S\)
    Looking at the map, there is no direct one-way route from \(R\) to \(S\). The only valid path is to go through city \(Q\) (\(R \to Q \to S\)):
    • At City \(R\): The person is ready at 7:00 AM. The train schedule box at \(R\) states that trains leave every \(60\text{ minutes}\) starting at 7:00 AM. The person can catch the 7:00 AM train immediately.
    • Arrival at \(Q\): Since travel takes 1 hour, they arrive at city \(Q\) at 8:00 AM.
    • At City \(Q\): They need to catch a train to \(S\). The schedule box at \(Q\) says trains leave every \(120\text{ minutes}\) starting at 5:00 AM. The available departure times are 5:00 AM, 7:00 AM, 9:00 AM, etc. Since the person arrived at 8:00 AM, they must wait until the next departure at 9:00 AM.
    • Arrival at \(S\): The train leaves at 9:00 AM and takes 1 hour, arriving at city \(S\) at 10:00 AM.
  2. Leg 2: Return from \(S\) to \(R\)
    Now, the person needs to travel from \(S\) back to \(R\). The available one-way routes require going through city \(P\) (\(S \to P \to R\)):
    • At City \(S\): The person is ready at 10:00 AM. The schedule box at \(S\) says trains leave every \(45\text{ minutes}\) starting at 8:00 AM. The departure times are 8:00 AM, 8:45 AM, 9:30 AM, 10:15 AM, etc. The person can catch the 10:15 AM train.
    • Arrival at \(P\): The train takes 1 hour, arriving at city \(P\) at 11:15 AM.
    • At City \(P\): They need to catch the final train back to \(R\). The schedule box at \(P\) says trains leave every \(90\text{ minutes}\) starting at 8:00 AM. The departure times are 8:00 AM, 9:30 AM, 11:00 AM, 12:30 PM, etc. Since they arrived at 11:15 AM, they must wait until the 12:30 PM train.
    • Arrival back at \(R\): The train leaves at 12:30 PM and takes 1 hour, arriving at the final destination city \(R\) at 1:30 PM.
Now, calculate the total elapsed time from the initial departure at 7:00 AM to the final arrival back at 1:30 PM: \[\text{Total Time} = 1:30\text{ PM} - 7:00\text{ AM} = 6\text{ hours and } 30\text{ minutes}\] This matches choice A perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{A. 6 hours 30 minutes}}\]
Key points
  • Network routing problems with fixed departure schedules are solved by tracking arrivals step-by-step and calculating the next available departure time using the scheduling interval constraints (\(T_{\text{start}} + n \cdot \Delta t\)).

questions.question: Equal sized circular regions are shaded in a square sheet of paper of 1 cm side length. Two cases, case M and case N, are considered as shown in the figures below. In the case M, four circles are shaded in the square sheet and in the case N, nine circles are shaded in the square sheet as shown. What is the ratio of the areas of unshaded regions of case M to that of case N?
questions.explanation:
We are given a square sheet of paper with a side length of \(s = 1\text{ cm}\) (\(\text{Area}_{\text{square}} = 1 \times 1 = 1\text{ cm}^2\)). Two different circle-shading configurations are applied inside this square, as shown in Fig. Q22.8.10:
  • Case M: Contains 4 identical shaded circles packed in a \(2 \times 2\) arrangement.
  • Case N: Contains 9 identical shaded circles packed in a \(3 \times 3\) arrangement.
We need to find the ratio of the areas of the unshaded regions of Case M to that of Case N. Let us calculate the total shaded area for both cases step-by-step:
  1. Analysis of Case M (\(2 \times 2\) grid):
    • Two circles span across the total side length \(s = 1\text{ cm}\), which means the diameter of a single circle is \(d_M = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{ cm}\). Its radius is \(r_M = \dfrac{1}{4}\text{ cm}\).
    • Calculate the total combined area of these 4 circles: \[A_{\text{shaded, M}} = 4 \times \Big( \pi r_M^2 \Big) = 4 \times \pi \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{\pi}{16} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2\]
  2. Analysis of Case N (\(3 \times 3\) grid):
    • Three circles span across the total side length \(s = 1\text{ cm}\), which means the diameter of a single circle is \(d_N = \dfrac{1}{3}\text{ cm}\). Its radius is \(r_N = \dfrac{1}{6}\text{ cm}\).
    • Calculate the total combined area of these 9 circles: \[A_{\text{shaded, N}} = 9 \times \Big( \pi r_N^2 \Big) = 9 \times \pi \left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 = 9 \times \dfrac{\pi}{36} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2\]
Notice that the total shaded area is exactly identical in both cases (\(A_{\text{shaded, M}} = A_{\text{shaded, N}} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)). Since the total area of the square sheet is the same (\(1\text{ cm}^2\)), the areas of the remaining unshaded regions must also be completely identical: \[A_{\text{unshaded, M}} = A_{\text{unshaded, N}} = 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\] Therefore, the ratio of their unshaded areas is exactly \(1 : 1\), which corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 1:1}}\]
Key points
  • Circle Packing Area Invariant: When identical circles are tightly packed inside a square frame in an \(n \times n\) arrangement, the total area covered by the circles remains completely constant, regardless of the value of \(n\). This property guarantees that the remaining unshaded area is always the same.
